content: Covance Inc., headquartered in Princeton, New Jersey, specializes in drug development and animal testing services. According to its website, it is one of the largest companies of its kind globally, generating annual revenues exceeding $1 billion, operating in 20 countries, and employing over 8,000 individuals worldwide. The company boasts the world’s largest central laboratory network and employs a global team of clinical trial professionals and cardiac safety experts. Covance became a publicly traded company in 1997 after being spun off by Corning Inc. Under the name Covance Research Products Inc. (CRP), based in Denver, Pennsylvania, the company also engages in the import and sale of laboratory animals and is the world’s largest breeder of laboratory dogs. It owns two dog-breeding facilities, two primate centers, and a rabbit-breeding facility. However, the company has faced controversy over allegations of primate abuse in its laboratories in Germany and the United States, as well as concerns related to a potential Ebola virus outbreak. History of Covance In the late 1980s and early 1990s, Corning Incorporated acquired several leading drug development companies, some with origins dating back to the 1940s. Covance primarily serves the pharmaceutical and biotech industries, offering testing services to the environmental, food, and nutritional supplement sectors. It also provides custom antibody products and services to the research community, particularly for neurological disorders. Covance offers cell type-specific marker antibodies for neuroscience, product suites for Alzheimer’s and Parkinson’s diseases, and an online antibody store featuring phospho-specific and secondary antibodies. Ebola Virus In October 1989, 100 cynomolgus macaques (Macaca fascicularis) were imported from Mindanao Island in the Philippines to Hazleton Research Products' (now Covance) Primate Quarantine Unit in Reston, Virginia. A second shipment from the same supplier arrived on November 8. Shortly thereafter, some monkeys were found to be infected with the Ebola virus. In January 1990, the same supplier sent another shipment of 100 macaques to Hazleton’s Texas Primate Center in Alice, Texas, and another 100 to the Reston unit. Between February 1 and March 15, 46 of 52 monkeys in one quarantine room died, exhibiting symptoms consistent with simian hemorrhagic fever and Ebola. In March 1996, 100 macaques from the same supplier were shipped to Hazleton in Alice, Texas, where two monkeys tested positive for the Ebola virus. Alleged Primate Abuse Münster, Germany In 2004, German journalist Friedrich Mülln worked undercover at Covance’s facility in Münster, Europe’s largest primate-testing center, and documented alleged abuse of monkeys and other non-human primates. The Münster laboratory specializes in reproduction toxicology and primate toxicology, including testing on pregnant primates. Covance is responsible for approximately half of the primate experiments conducted in Germany. Undercover footage revealed staff making monkeys dance to loud pop music, handling them roughly, and shouting at them. The monkeys were shown isolated in small wire cages with little or no natural light or environmental enrichment, and exposed to high noise levels caused by staff shouting and playing the radio. Primatologist Dr. Jane Goodall described the living conditions as horrendous and stated that seeing the monkeys crazed with boredom and sadness was deeply, deeply disturbing. Primatologist Stephen Brend criticized the use of stressed monkeys in experiments, calling it bad science and stating that obtaining reliable data under such conditions was untenable. Publicity in Germany led to the Close Covance (Covance Schliessen) animal rights campaign, as well as campaigns in Britain by the British Union for the Abolition of Vivisection (BUAV) and in America by PETA. Following the release of the footage on German television, local authorities in Münster inspected Covance and required the installation of video cameras to monitor staff working with primates. Covance appealed the decision, and the courts ruled that video monitoring would infringe on staff rights. The public prosecutor’s office reviewed the footage and questioned witnesses but concluded that Covance had not committed any prosecutable offenses, clearing the company of all charges. Covance claimed that the editing of the footage exaggerated the evidence. After parts of Mülln’s footage were aired on German television and published in major newspapers, Covance filed a lawsuit, leading a German court to ban further distribution of the material. However, a higher court later ruled that the public’s right to be informed outweighed the company’s privacy rights, allowing the footage to be displayed publicly, though not in its original television-edited form or by animal rights groups. Vienna, Virginia During an undercover investigation in 2004-2005, PETA found similar conditions at Covance’s Vienna, Virginia laboratory. A former employee, who worked there from 2002 to 2004, alleged that monkeys were dissected while still alive and capable of feeling pain. These allegations surfaced as part of an open-records request made by PETA in November 2006. The employee had previously approached city officials in Chandler, Arizona, with her concerns after learning that Covance planned to build a new laboratory there. She claimed that three monkeys in the Vienna laboratory had pushed themselves up on their elbows and gasped for breath after their eyes had been removed and their intestines were being extracted during necropsies. When she raised concerns at a study directors' meeting, she was told that the movements were merely reflexes. She believed these movements indicated botched euthanasia performed by inadequately trained personnel. The employee reported being ridiculed and subjected to veiled threats when she contacted her supervisors about the issue. In June 2005, Covance filed a lawsuit against PETA and its former employee for fraud, breach of employee contract, and conspiracy to harm the company’s business by deceitfully infiltrating and videotaping the company’s Vienna, Virginia facility. Covance and PETA reached a settlement in which PETA agreed to a five-year ban on attempts to infiltrate Covance facilities. Inspections by the United States Department of Agriculture (USDA) resulted in 16 citations, which Covance described as ranging from administrative issues to scope of veterinary authority. The company agreed to pay a settlement of $8,720. Expansion In recent years, Covance has expanded through acquisitions of drug development companies. Notably, in August 2005, Covance acquired GFI Clinical Services, an 80-bed clinical pharmacology business, from West Pharmaceutical Services, Inc., to enhance its Phase I clinical research offerings. Covance also acquired a provider of monoclonal antibodies used in cancer, infectious disease, and neurodegenerative disease research.
